parsed_answer.content: The Thundering Herd problem occurs in distributed systems and high-concurrency Java applications when a large number of threads or processes wake up simultaneously to compete for a resource that has just become available or expired. In a typical cache-aside pattern, if a popular key expires, multiple concurrent requests will see a cache miss and all attempt to recompute the value by hitting the underlying database simultaneously. This creates a massive, unnecessary spike in latency and CPU load, effectively turning a simple cache miss into a potential system-wide outage. Preventing this requires shifting from a 'first-come, first-served' race condition to a controlled synchronization strategy that ensures only one thread performs the expensive computation while others either wait or serve stale data.

items: Double-Checked Locking: Use a volatile variable to check the cache state, then synchronize on a monitor object. The second check inside the synchronized block ensures that only the first thread performs the work, while subsequent threads see the newly populated cache.

Probabilistic Early Recomputation (XFetch): Instead of waiting for a hard expiration, attach a random 'probabilistic' expiry to the cache key. Threads calculate a 'delta' based on the time remaining; if the random check fails, the thread refreshes the cache early, effectively spreading the load over time.

Mutex/Semaphore Guarding: Use a 'lock-per-key' approach with a ConcurrentHashMap of locks. This allows fine-grained synchronization where only threads requesting the same specific key are blocked, preventing global application lock contention.

Stale-While-Revalidate: Configure your cache provider to return the expired value for a short window while a background thread asynchronously refreshes the data, ensuring the user never experiences the latency of the recomputation.

parsed_answer.content: Beware of 'lock striping' overhead. While using a ConcurrentHashMap of locks prevents global contention, creating millions of lock objects can lead to significant GC pressure. Always use a fixed-size pool of locks or a dedicated library like Guava's Striped<Lock> to manage memory footprint in high-throughput systems.

title: How to prevent the "Thundering Herd" problem?
